title: Enterprise Password Management Guide: How to Choose the Right Security & Compliance Platform
description: Practical enterprise password management guidance with planning steps, selection criteria, risks, and operational checks.
author: Marcus Rivera

sections.title: Inventory credentials and use cases
sections.body: Identify how employees, administrators, service accounts, contractors, and teams currently store and share passwords, API keys, recovery codes, and secrets. Separate human login credentials from machine secrets because they may need different controls and rotation policies. Record the systems with the greatest impact if an account is compromised and the recovery steps required to regain access.

sections.title: Set security requirements before selecting a vendor
sections.body: Define requirements for SSO, MFA, SCIM provisioning, role-based access, shared vaults, audit events, emergency access, device policies, and offboarding. Verify which capabilities are included in each plan and which require add-ons. Test access using different roles, not only an administrator account. A product's general security description does not prove that the chosen plan supports every required control.

sections.title: Test onboarding and offboarding
sections.body: Run the full lifecycle for a new employee, a contractor, a team transfer, and a departing administrator. Confirm that vault access is provisioned and revoked correctly, shared credentials are transferred or rotated, and recovery remains possible without a single individual. Define what happens to shared items when an owner leaves and how exceptions are approved.

sections.title: Manage shared and privileged secrets
sections.body: Use separate vaults or collections for privileged credentials, production access, and ordinary team logins. Apply least privilege and avoid shared administrator accounts when named accounts are available. Define how emergency access works, how secrets are rotated, and how usage is audited. Do not store secrets in notes, browser bookmarks, or unprotected exports just because a vault is available.

sections.title: Evaluate recovery and availability
sections.body: Test account recovery, device loss, employee departure, service outage, and administrator lockout. Understand which recovery methods bypass normal controls and how they are monitored. Confirm export behavior and how the organization would retrieve credentials if the vendor relationship ends. Recovery must be secure and usable under pressure, not a procedure known only to one administrator.

sections.title: Review compliance, privacy, and vendor terms
sections.body: Check encryption design, administrator access, audit retention, data location, support access, incident notification, subprocessors, and deletion behavior. Review current documentation and contracts with security, privacy, and legal owners. Confirm whether logs expose credential names or other sensitive metadata. Keep a record of the evidence reviewed and the residual risks accepted.

sections.title: Plan rollout and adoption
sections.body: Pilot with a team that has a mix of technical and non-technical users. Measure successful enrollment, password reuse reduction where measurable, support requests, recovery issues, and completion of offboarding tasks. Provide short instructions for importing existing credentials safely and deleting insecure copies. Avoid forcing a bulk migration until the team has tested how duplicates and shared items are handled.

sections.title: Purchase checklist
sections.body: Proceed when access policies, lifecycle controls, recovery, audit visibility, migration, and pricing are validated. Assign an owner for vault structure, administrator access, incident response, and periodic access review. Reassess after changes to identity systems, contractor use, or the threat model. A password manager is a control within a wider identity program, not a substitute for MFA, least privilege, and incident readiness.
